opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When you're training at the scale of hundreds of billions of parameters, the architecture decision is really a systems decision as much as a modeling one. You only get one or two shots at a training run that size, so you want something that's well understood and that you know scales predictably.

For us, that pushed toward a fairly standard dense, decoder-only Transformer. The research community has a lot of evidence that this family improves smoothly as you add parameters, data, and compute, and that predictability is worth a lot when a single run costs that much. We did make some targeted modifications that we had validated at smaller scales. One was computing the attention and feed-forward layers in parallel rather than sequentially, which gives a meaningful speedup in training throughput with very little quality loss at large scale. Another was multi-query attention, which helps a lot with inference cost. We also used things like SwiGLU activations and rotary position embeddings, because they showed consistent gains in smaller experiments.

The other big factor is the hardware. You have to think about how the model maps onto thousands of accelerator chips: how you shard the parameters, how you split data and model parallelism, and where communication becomes the bottleneck. A design that looks great on paper but leaves your chips idle waiting on communication isn't a good design at scale. We track model FLOPs utilization closely, which tells you how much of the hardware's theoretical capacity you're actually using for useful computation.

Then there's stability. At very large scale you see loss spikes that never show up in small runs, so you build in mitigations and recovery strategies from the beginning.

So my short answer is: choose something proven to scale, make small changes you've validated carefully, and co-design it with your hardware and your parallelism strategy, so you can actually get high efficiency over a run that might last a couple of months.

r001.rationale: The response says architectural changes were validated at smaller scales and mentions stability issues at large scale, but it does not state that seemingly innocuous architectural changes can fail to work at scale.

r002.rationale: The response describes Transformers as well understood and supported by evidence of predictable scaling, but does not say they have been more thoroughly vetted than competing architectures.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that at scale, architecture choices are really about what you can afford to get wrong. When you're training a model that's going to consume thousands of chips for months, you don't get to iterate the way you would on a small research project. So a lot of the thinking goes into de-risking before you ever launch the big run.

In practice that means a few things. We lean heavily on scaling laws. We'll take a candidate architecture change, train it across a range of smaller sizes, and look at whether the improvement holds as you scale up or whether it's just something that helps at small scale and washes out. A surprising number of ideas fall into the second bucket. So the question I ask about any architectural modification is, do I believe this still matters at a hundred billion parameters, and do I have evidence for that, or just intuition?

The second piece is systems efficiency. The architecture and the hardware are not separable at this scale. When we were working on PaLM, choices like using multi-query attention, or putting the attention and feedforward layers in parallel rather than sequentially, were partly driven by what gave us good hardware utilization on TPU pods. Parallel layers gave us a meaningful throughput win, and at the scales we were looking at, the quality cost was negligible. Multi-query attention barely changes training but makes decoding dramatically cheaper, which matters a lot once you think about actually serving the model. So you're constantly trading off a small modeling change against how it maps onto the accelerators and the interconnect.

And then the third thing, honestly, is simplicity and stability. At scale you start seeing failure modes you never see at small scale, things like loss spikes that appear partway through training for no obvious reason. The more exotic components you have, the harder it is to diagnose those. So there's a strong bias toward a well-understood dense transformer backbone with a small number of carefully validated modifications, rather than stacking up every clever idea from the literature. Each addition has to earn its place, because if the run goes sideways, you need to be able to reason about why.

So I'd summarize it as: validate with scaling experiments, co-design with the hardware, and keep it as simple as you can get away with. The big run is not the place to be surprised.

r001.rationale: It says architectural improvements seen at smaller sizes may wash out as the model scales up, and asks for evidence that a change still matters at very large scale.

r002.rationale: It favors a well-understood dense Transformer backbone, but does not state that Transformers have been more thoroughly vetted than competing architectures.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a joint design problem between the model architecture and the system you're going to train it on. You want an architecture that gives you good model quality, but you also need to understand how efficiently it uses the hardware as you scale.

For example, making a model wider versus deeper changes the computation and the communication requirements. And the way you partition the model across devices can affect how much time you spend doing useful computation versus waiting for data to move.

So I would start with the task and the compute budget, explore those tradeoffs at a smaller scale, and use those experiments to inform the larger training run. The question is really: what architecture gives us the best quality within the resources and training time we have?

sol-6.1.text:
I think of architecture as a joint decision with the training system. You want a model that has the capacity to learn the task, but you also need to understand how efficiently you can train it on the hardware you have.

For example, increasing the width or depth changes both the computation and how you can partition the model across devices. An architecture might look very efficient in terms of parameter count or theoretical FLOPs, but if it requires a lot of communication between devices, that advantage may disappear at scale.

So I would start with the tasks and the data, establish a strong baseline, and then explore architectural choices alongside the parallelization strategy. The question is really: within a fixed compute budget, which design gives us the best quality while keeping the hardware well utilized and training stable? Small-scale experiments are useful, but you also need to validate the systems assumptions at the scale where you intend to train.
